title: Ramon.Space raises $124m Series B after claiming “Earth-grade” computing in space
html:
Space computing integrator Ramon.Space has announced a $124 million Series B, led by PSG Equity, to accelerate its development of onboard computing systems, emphasizing its exposure to the AI boom.

"We have proven that Earth-grade computing works in space, and we are delivering it today," said Avi Shabtai, CEO of Ramon.Space, in a statement. "We are paving the way for a new industry, and customer demand is growing quickly. This funding can help us scale to create the computing foundation that will serve the space economy's accelerated growth."

Ramon.Space described the challenge of withstanding radiation, extreme temperatures, and power constraints of space, and alluded to its history pre-dating the ODC craze in which it supported commercial and government Earth observation enterprises across the world such as Eutelsat OneWeb, and SES Space & Defence.

The company intends to use the new money to scale production and accelerate its pipeline.

US-Israeli company Ramon.Space asserted in press material that inference workloads were moving into orbit, stating: “The line between Earth and space computing infrastructure is disappearing.”

To date, ODC developers have only tested demonstrations on prototype compute satellites, such as Sophia Space, which last week deployed its operating system for the first time.

While “Earth-grade” processing has always been possible in space, this has never been the obstacle to making compute more commercially viable in orbit than terrestrially, with orbital downlink being the biggest obstacle among many.

Compute? In my orbit?

Last week, yet another obstacle joined the pile, as the FT reported lenders Apollo and Goldman Sachs, among others, aimed to bar SpaceX from launching $40 billion of chips into orbit aboard its one-million-satellite ODC constellation concept Starcloud, as launching the collateral into space would prevent them from reclaiming and selling the semiconductors in the event of default.

Ramon.Space’s own financiers, joining PSG in the pre-seed, included new investors from Micron Technology, Senvest, and Phoenix Financial, alongside existing investors including StageOne, Deep Insight, and Grove Ventures.

“We're proud to partner with Avi and his team to bring this technology to a broader market and help shape the future of computing in space,” said Ronen Nir, managing director at PSG, in a statement.

It remains to be seen if PSG and the other funds in the round will forbid Ramon.Space from wasting precious semiconductors by installing them into satellites and shooting them into space instead of keeping them safe and sound for potential repossession, as leading US institutions are reportedly intending to do with the world’s leading space company.
summary: Compute integrator to scale the creation of the processing foundation to accelerate the space economy
